items.title: Software Bonkers
items.summary: Craig Mod built two pieces of software he'd wanted for years — a social platform for his membership community and a five-day tax accounting tool — using AI coding assistance, arguing that the tools have crossed a threshold where a determined non-programmer can now ship working software tailored precisely to their own needs and data.
items.why: Mod's hands-on account of what the AI-coding threshold actually feels like maps directly to how Manik is approaching his own builds; the argument for bespoke, data-owning software over subscription tools has practical implications for how Cuemath frames internal design tooling decisions.

items.title: Templo's visual identity for DeafCity Hub is a fusion of creative coding, British sign language and gestural motion capture
items.summary: London studio Templo built the brand identity for DeafCity Hub, a Deaf cultural space, using motion-capture of real British Sign Language gestures to generate animated letterforms — the modular typeface has ten characters, one per finger, so the mark literally moves the way the community communicates.
items.why: A rare example of animation built into a brand system at its foundation rather than as a decorative afterthought — the principle of deriving motion from meaningful actions directly informs how Cuemath's gamification animations could work: XP gain, belt progression, and reward moments that move in ways that feel earned, not generic.

items.title: Ask LukeW: Less Walls of Text
items.summary: Luke Wroblewski describes how he solved the text-wall problem in his AI design Q&A app: he used an AI model to combine auto-generated image titles with hand-written accessibility descriptions from his archive, producing search-friendly labels that let the app retrieve and embed relevant visuals in answers — one AI layer improving another's output.
items.why: The insight that AI metadata quality gates the entire retrieval experience is immediately applicable to any content-heavy product — directly relevant to how Cuemath could structure its practice-content library if AI starts generating or surfacing math problems and explanations.

items.title: From YWCA to Hotel Willo: how Rethink solved one of branding's trickiest problems
items.summary: Toronto agency Rethink rebranded a Vancouver hotel from YWCA Hotel — a name that made people assume it was a shelter — to Hotel Willo, using a willow-tree silhouette as a minimal looping symbol, vibrant colors, and a playful but practical voice to signal boutique hospitality without a heavy concept.
items.why: The brief was pure brand disambiguation: help audiences understand what a product is before they can care about it — the exact challenge MathGym faces whenever it needs to signal 'math practice app' rather than 'homework help' or 'tutoring'; Rethink's restraint over concept-heavy solutions is the right model.

items.title: Show me the work
items.summary: A short, pointed essay arguing that job titles in tech are used to signal hierarchy rather than ambition, and that only actual output is credible — uses AOC and Wolverine as references for what professional authority that doesn't need a label looks like.
items.why: Sharp shorthand for how design credibility is built in a product org: in an environment where the design function competes for influence, Rendle's case for output-over-title is a useful anchor when building a team or making cases to stakeholders at Cuemath.
